h1: Metformin vs insulin: how much each lowers A1C, and how they differ
dek: Metformin lowers A1C by about 1.1 percentage points on its own; insulin can lower it as far as needed but brings low blood sugar and weight gain. Here is what the trials measured for each, and when the 2026 ADA Standards use one, the other, or both.
scope: Informational intent only. Cost and pharmacy queries are not mapped.

outline.heading: How metformin and insulin work differently
outline.html:
Metformin does not add insulin to the body. Its label describes three actions: it lowers the amount of glucose the liver releases, reduces how much glucose the gut absorbs, and makes muscle and other tissue respond better to the insulin already there {glucophage}. Because it does not push insulin levels up, it rarely drives glucose too low on its own {ada9}.

Insulin is the hormone itself. Injected insulin moves glucose into cells whatever the person's own insulin output, which is why it works when the pancreas makes too little and why too large a dose for the food eaten produces hypoglycemia {ada9}. That difference in mechanism explains most of the differences in the table below: metformin has a natural limit to how far it lowers A1C, and insulin does not, but insulin needs dose adjustment and glucose monitoring.
